input: It is important to note that decisions around staffing levels are rarely straightforward, and the maintenance crew's current situation is no exception. At present, the crew comprises 18 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 8% of paid hours, a level that many would regard as significant. One option under consideration is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, thereby reducing the reliance on overtime working. However, it is worth noting that such a hire would cost $87k per year on a fully loaded basis, and this cost would be incurred throughout the year. By contrast, the overtime itself is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, meaning that for much of the year demand is considerably lower. This creates a complex picture involving cost, coverage, and flexibility, and decision-makers will need to weigh these factors carefully. In summary, while the $87k hire may offer benefits in terms of peak coverage and reduced pressure on existing staff, a thorough and balanced assessment will be essential before any commitment is made, and further analysis of the seasonal pattern would undoubtedly be valuable in informing the final decision. It goes without saying that any change to the establishment would also have knock-on effects for training, supervision, and holiday cover, all of which would need to be carefully planned for well in advance of any change taking effect.
target: Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $87k per year fully loaded, and on last year's paid-hours record the exchange is not justified on cost: the overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, while a hire is paid for the full year. The maintenance crew has 18 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 8% of paid hours last year. The pattern of the overtime matters more than its size. Hours bought through a hire arrive evenly across the year, but the demand for them does not: the peaks need extra hands for short periods, and between peaks the crew covers its planned work within normal hours. A hire therefore relieves the peaks only by adding capacity that stands idle for much of the year, and the annual cost buys the idle time along with the peak cover. The trade-off is $87k per year, every year, against overtime that arises only in the peak windows. Maintenance management should establish how much of the peak overtime is movable before the establishment is increased. Planned work that can be rescheduled out of the peak windows reduces overtime without a permanent addition to cost; work fixed by the production calendar cannot move, and for that share a hire is the dependable cover. The recommendation is that maintenance management quantify the movable share of the overtime and bring the hire forward only for the share that cannot be moved.
